https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: The destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships. Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Reuters View image in fullscreen The destroyer HMS Duncan, pictured in Portsmouth Harbour, was one of three Royal Navy vessels deployed to monitor Russian ships. Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Reuters Military Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK waters Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel Geraldine McKelvie Sat 29 Aug 2026 11.06 EDT First published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 09.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters, it has emerged. The “intense” 72-hour operation took place last week, with radars used to monitor four ships that made their way from the North Sea through to the Channel. The fleet was surveilled by HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn, with a Merlin helicopter providing support, officials said. The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was observed escorting the cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, which are under sanctions, towards Dover. In response, Russia deployed its own military resources, including the Neustrashimy frigate, to guard the shipment. Gen Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continued to pose “an unacceptable risk” to UK security. “Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose,” he said. “That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.” The Royal Navy recently warned of increasing Russian activity in UK waters . In July, it spent 21 days monitoring ships from Moscow, an increase of 25% compared with the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly observed warships in the Dover strait and the North Sea. In June, the Royal Marines seized the Russian tanker Smyrtos , the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel, one of more than 500 that have been sanctioned by the UK. The Kremlin has threatened the UK after Andy Burnham visited Kyiv this week in his first overseas trip as prime minister. During the trip, Burnham said the UK would provide Ukraine with military support, including blueprints for components of long-range Scalp missiles. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Although western officials have tried to play down the prospect of direct conflict between Russia and Nato, the Kremlin has accused the UK and its allies of “playing with fire” in relation to their continued support for Ukraine. Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian foreign minister, said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources”. https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/9.text: This EV can travel 936km on a single charge With the aim of putting the once dreaded concept of 'range anxiety' firmly in the rear view mirrors it seems electric vehicle hypermiling is a key promotional focus for carmakers around the world. Subscribe now for unlimited access. Login or signup to continue reading Skoda is the latest brand to wring an extreme number of kilometres from a single EV battery charge , with a team of drivers pushing the recently introduced pure-electric Skoda Peaq seven-seat SUV 936km from the company's Mladá Boleslav headquarters in northern Czechia, north-west through Germany to the Netherlands. The recently introduced Peaq already has an impressive WLTP-rated combined cycle (urban/extra-urban) range figure of 647 kilometres. Read more Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Kia EV9 will have company as incoming 2027 Skoda Peaq to arrive as a three-row family SUV 2026 Skoda Enyaq will likely be Skoda's most popular model and it gets big upgrades to take on 2026 Zeekr 7X and Tesla Model Y 'Overcooked': Lower sales the new normal said Skoda boss as Audi prepares for tough end to year Additional 289km of range Somehow the car's 91kWh battery was able to cough up an additional 289km of range, setting a new seven-seat EV range record in the process. The run was supervised by certification authority TÜV SÜD with average energy use coming in at 9.2kWh/100km, an exceptional number for a fully-equipped, three-row SUV weighing in excess of two tonnes. Despite its close to 4.9-metre overall length the Czech maker's new flagship boasts a drag-coefficient of 0.249, which surely assisted in the distance attempt. Testing new SUV's range potential Skoda said company employees, Marek Jež and Jakub Krs, wanted to test themselves and the new SUV's range potential. "The aim was to demonstrate what the technology can achieve when pushed to its limits. To maximise the range, we selected the most suitable route and, of course, adapted our driving style accordingly," said Jakub Krs (Head of high-voltage battery strategy at Škoda Auto). "In everyday use, customers are unlikely to drive the car this way. Instead, they will take advantage of everything the Peaq has to offer in terms of driving dynamics, onboard infotainment and comfort," added Marek Jež (Head of the Peaq model series). Standard car, standard rubber The car was a stock Peaq 90 which features the 91kWh traction battery (86kWh net), a single 210kW motor driving the rear wheels and its 19-inch wheels were shod with standard low-rolling-resistance rubber. Departing Mladá Boleslav (where the Peaq is produced) at midday on Tuesday August 25, the record team took breaks to change drivers, rest and eat before reaching the Netherlands early on the morning of Wednesday August 26. The big seven-seat electric SUV is expected to land in Australia in 2027, where it would complement the mid-size Enyaq and compact Elroq electric SUVs in Skoda's expanding local EV range. Based on European pricing it will likely sit above the $80,000 mark here, sending a shot across the bows of existing electric three-row SUVs like the Hyundai Ioniq 9 ($119,750) and Kia EV9 ($97,000), both before on-road costs. https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/19/meg.text: Menü Kereső Még kormányon sincs az AfD, már az oroszokkal tárgyalna olaj- és gázvásárlásról Gazdaság Alice Weidel, az AfD társelnöke kampánygyűlést tart Mecklenburg-Elő-Pomeránia közelgő tartományi választása előtt Neubrandenburgban, 2026, szeptember 18-án – Fotó: Lisi Niesner / Reuters Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Elkezdődtek az egyeztetések a felméréseket vezető német AfD (Alternatíva Németországért) párt és Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök megbízottja közt a gázszállítások újraindításáról – értesült a Reuters pénteken két, a tervet ismerő embertől. Mindez azért érdekes, mert a szélsőjobboldali párt nincs kormányon, bár regionális szinten már előretört, nemrég Szász-Anhalt tartományban nyert választást . Az AfD hírhedten jó kapcsolatokat ápol egyébként a Kremllel. A Reuters forrásai szerint orosz részről Kirill Dmitrijev, Putyin közeli tanácsadója, német részről Alice Weidel és Tino Chrupalla AfD-társelnökök vennének részt a legkésőbb 2027 márciusában megtartandó találkozón. Mindkét fél elutasította, hogy kommentálja az értesüléseket. Úgy tudni, a találkozó feltétele, hogy Oroszország és Ukrajna megállapodjon egy békeegyezményben. A csúcson az Egyesült Államok is képviseltethetné magát, akár a nemrég Moszkvában járt küldöttekkel, Steve Witkoffal és Jared Kushnerrel. Helyszínként felmerült Izrael, az Egyesült Arab Emirátusok és India is. Ukrajna 2022-es orosz lerohanása előtt Oroszországból érkezett Németország nyersolajának harmada, földgázának több mint fele. Ezt aztán a minimálisra csavarták le, amiben az Északi Áramlat tenger alatti gázvezeték – valószínűleg ukrán – felrobbantása is szerepet játszott. Weidel jó ideje hangoztatja, hogy fel kell hagyni az orosz energiahordozók bojkottjával. Pártja szerint ideje lenne újranyitni az Északi Áramlatot is, mivel Németország azóta keresgéli az olaj- és gázimportja rentábilis forrásait. A Reuters megjegyzi, ugyan a moszkvai Amerikai Kereskedelmi Kamara üdvözölte a közeledést, Németország kelet-európai szövetségesei nem örülnének neki. Otthon sem mindenki boldog, Michael Kellner, a Zöldek képviselője szerint nem követhetik el még egyszer ugyanezt a hibát, „ez hazaárulás lenne”. Hozzátette, Putyin az AfD-t saját céljaira használja. A kereszténydemokrata (CDU-s) Roderich Kiesewetter azt mondta, Putyin hibrid fegyverként használja az olajat és gázt. A Reuters felidézi még, a szovjet megszállás alatti Kelet-Németországban a mai napig sokan szimpatizálnak Oroszországgal. Dmitrijev egyébként az X-en már jelezte, voltaképp szurkol az AfD-nek a következő tartományi választáson Mecklenburg-Elő-Pomerániában. Szerinte egy kiszámíthatóan működő Északi Áramlat megfizethetővé tenné az életet, alacsonyabb energiaszámlákhoz, több munkahelyhez és nagyobb növekedéshez járulna hozzá. „Nem kell több német energiaügyi és ipari öngyilkosság” – tette hozzá, megosztva Weidel egy posztját. https://www.wglt.org/local-news/2026-09-.text: Sign In Sign In On Air Now Playing WGLT Local News Having Sept. 11 birthdays calls for preserving personal joy while honoring collective grief WGLT | By Michele Steinbacher Published September 10, 2026 at 4:46 PM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 7:30 Michele Steinbacher / WGLT From left, Joan Smeltzer, of Fairbury; Jo and Brian Hundman, their daughter Carley Hundman Rugaard, and Carley's 6-month-old son, Sonny Rugaard, all of Bloomington; Paige Buschman, of Bloomington; and Ryan Bliss of rural Towanda. Smeltzer, Hundman Rugaard, Buschman and Bliss all have Sept. 11 birthdays. Notably, Jo Hundman gave birth to Carley at St. Joseph Medical Center in Bloomington 25 years ago, just hours after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Chances are you know lots of people who have September birthdays. Nine of the 10 most common days to have birthdays in the U.S. happen this month . So, for most of our nation’s history, having a Sept. 11 birthday was unremarkable. That changed in 2001. Now such a birthday means an unwanted tie to the worst terrorist attack in U.S. history . [I should know, it's my birthday too.] Bloomington resident Paige Buschman, who turned 6 that year, said, it’s just been part of life for her. “If you say ‘My birthday’s 9/11’ people are like ‘Wow, really?.’ I’ve had multiple occasions, like, there was often commenting on it, some way or another — whether it was ‘Oh, I’m sorry,’ or ‘Ewww, yikes,” she said. Except for New York City, where the immediate impact of the attacks has been most direct — the somber anniversary has faded from its earlier emotional intensity. But 25 years later scholars still are unpacking how 9/11 changed America , in the broadest of terms. People with Sept. 11 birthdays continue to find themselves seeking a balance of retaining personal joy with the nation’s collective fear, anger and grief surrounding it all. One of those is Ryan Bliss, a digital artist who lives in rural Towanda. In 2001, he lived in San Diego. His 30th birthday started with unexpected news. Bliss’ mother — back in Central Illinois — called surprisingly early, at around 6 a.m. Pacific time. Her first words weren’t “Happy Birthday” but rather an urgent “Turn on the TV.” Any plans for celebrating disappeared quickly. In the days, months and years that followed, Bliss said it became clear the country had hit a turning point. “On the totem pole of being affected by 9/11, having your birthday ruined is probably the lowest,” said Bliss, adding, “But you know it’s still there.” He and others interviewed for this story say the birthday is an interesting connection, albeit trivial. This is especially true considering the thousands of lives lost due to the attacks, as well as the radiating loss felt by their family and friends, noted Bliss. A person can pick any terrible event from history, and that would fall on people’s birthdays, and other anniversaries. But why is there such a strong connection to this one? Maybe it’s because the date itself is the name. An early push with the federal government labeling it Patriot Day never really took hold among the populace, and it had its critics . Now, 9/11 is the term for the attacks. “I can't remember a date in history, you know, other than Dec. 7, 1941 — when Pearl Harbor was attacked — that the date itself is such an inextricably linked part of the tragedy,” said Bliss. “I mean, here it is, still called 9/11.” The trend could be changing though. Most people now recognize Jan. 6 as the 2021 insurrection at the U.S. Capitol; and Oct. 7 as shorthand for the 2023 Hamas attack in Israel. Adam Gray / AP A 'Never Forget' wrist band is left on the 9/11 Memorial, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026 in New York. (AP Photo/Adam Gray) Changing generations mean fewer who knew 9/11 firsthand Retired speech pathologist Joan Smeltzer, of Fairbury, turned 49 on Sept. 11, 2001. She was working in a Piper City school, when she learned about the attacks. For several years after, the mere mention of her birthday drew unwanted attention. “If you'd go someplace and you'd have to tell someone your birthday, they'd all go ‘Ahh’ and give you this big-eyed stare,” she said. That made her feel torn. She said she understood people’s negative associations. But inside, she was happy it was her birthday. Smeltzer says she’s noticed the commenting has tapered off in the past decade, which she attributes to a subsiding of the collective trauma Americans experienced in 2001 — or maybe a generational shift. About a third of Americans weren’t even alive. And millions more were too young to remember. Paige Buschman, associate director for Illinois State University’s Center for Civic Engagement, said that's true for most younger people. “The difference between Gen Z and Millennial is whether or not you remember life before 9/11,” she said, adding “I'm literally considered right on the cusp,” with her Sept. 11, 1995, birthday. She was young but remembers a few key details of that day in 2001: When she arrived at her morning kindergarten session in Lemont, she was a bit giddy as the birthday girl. Buschman remembers the mood turning quickly though. As the adults became frazzled and upset, she felt the need to tamp down her excitement. Soon after, all the kids were sent home. “They didn’t tell us what was going on, we were too young,” she noted. Growing up, she remembers September 11ths marked by moments of silence in school, and a relatively somber tone. She wonders if the impact of it all played a role in her becoming a sociologist, and working in civic engagement. This month, her office has been organizing a campus-led Saturday of Service for this weekend. Buschman thinks telling people she has a Sept. 11 birthday creates a moment where they want to share with her: “It almost immediately sparks a conversation of ‘Where were you on 9/11. I feel like I've sort of like curated histories of 9/11 experiences.” A baby born into a chaotic world Michele Steinbacher / WGLT Jo and Briand Hundman, their daughter Carley Hundman Rugaard, and Carley's 6-month-old son, Sonny Rugaard, all of Bloomington. Jo Hundman gave birth to Carley at St. Joseph Medical Center in Bloomington 25 years ago, just hours after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. When someone asks Jo Hundman where she was on 9/11, her answer is a real attention grabber: She was giving birth. The real estate agent and her husband Brian Hundman, a Growmark executive, both live in Bloomington, and are the parents of three adult children. The couple arrived early that morning at St. Joseph Medical Center, and got settled in a labor and delivery room. “And then, I was watching the second plane fly into the World Trade Center — live on TV, while I was in labor,” said Jo. It was way too much, she said. They decided to turn off the TV and shut out the negativity. About five hours later, their second child, a daughter they named Carley, was born. “You know, we always say she was a blessing on a bad day,” said Jo, with Brian adding, “A tragic day in the world. But obviously, for us, you know, such a joy.” That happiness was tempered by the grief and fear that was everywhere as the day unfolded. Brian recalls looking out from the maternity ward, to see Eastland Mall’s then-usually bustling parking lot eerily empty. And the hospital was mostly empty, too, with a skeletal staff and few, if any, visitors. Jo remembers struggling to process her happiness amid such surroundings. “Everyone was freaked out and depressed, and it was a really long night, the first night that she was born — thinking about bringing a child into such a crazy world,” she said. “I mean, even the nurses were crying,” she said, noting one of the OB nurses was worried about her son, who was serving in the military. 9/11 babies turn 25 Carley Hundman Rugaard was one of more than 13,000 babies born that day in America. Most of that group, like Hundman Rugaard, ended up having their own life-altering experience in high school, graduating the spring the COVID pandemic hit. That batch of babies turns 25 this week. A graduate of Central Catholic High School, Hundman Rugaard, now a stylist with Elevation Salon, lives in Bloomington. She learned early on about the significance of her birthday. Each September, the U.S. flags would come out, and 9/11 was the focus of school assemblies and history lessons. When she was 10, the Hundmans took part in a fundraiser for New York families directly affected by the attacks, and a year later, she joined some of her family on a trip to NYC, to visit the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. But mom Jo Hundman said, overall, they tried to keep the national anniversary out of the family celebrations. The goal was for Carley’s birthday to be as normal as her sister’s and brother’s. Among Hundman Rugaard’s most memorable birthdays was her 21st, when she was living in Phoenix. “I met another girl with the same exact birthday, and she was like, ‘Nobody gets what it's like to have a birthday on the 9/11,’ which, it was pretty cool to get someone else's perspective, too, of that day.” Adam Gray / AP People walk through the Empty Sky 9/11 Memorial, Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Jersey City, NJ. (AP Photo/Adam Gray) This year's birthday This year, many of us marking Sept. 11 birthdays will join the rest of the country in recognizing the 25th anniversary. We’ll follow retrospectives like the NPR one WGLT will air Friday evening, and documentaries that will be on TV. But the consensus is, there’s also room to celebrate our own joyous Sept. 11ths. Bliss and his wife Jessica will meet their grown sons for dinner in Eureka, and Smeltzer’s visiting an old college friend. Buschman’s taking time for herself, and making pierogis — a nod to her Polish heritage. For the Hundman family, it’s a full-circle moment. Their very own 9/11 baby Carley marks her first birthday as a mother herself. Carley wants to have a low-key birthday this weekend, spending time with her husband Tucker Rugaard and their 6-month-old, Sonny. “Now that we have a baby, you know, we get to enjoy him. That's a celebration every day,” she said. Bliss said each year as his birthday arrives, he heeds the advice his mother gave back on Sept. 11, 2001. "She told me just remember that it was a joyous day before this happened, and it should be for you. So, you have to learn to kind of compartmentalize what happened and have your day, but also remember, and don’t let the two intermingle too much,” said Bliss. As for this reporter, I'll go out with friends and family this weekend, but my Friday morning will be more introspective. I have a longtime birthday morning ritual of sipping my coffee and enjoying a distraction-free listening session of The Rising , Bruce Springsteen’s album reflecting on the 9/11 attacks and the year that followed. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian Poland Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living Will military spending help or hinder Poland’s growth story? Poland’s push for EU energy resilience amid Russian aggression Richard Partington in Warsaw Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.56 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades. For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history. For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity. View image in fullscreen Cezary Błaszczyk and Natalia Kasperska at the Varso Tower. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian “We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska. “Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says. Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. View image in fullscreen The Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose walks on a 500-metre-long tightrope stretched between the Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower on 31 May. Photograph: Sergei Gapon/AFP/Getty Images National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain. “Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister. Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law. However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped. Poland GDP per capita graphic For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote. Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived. Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record. On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy. Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe . “You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.” On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters. The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen. Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics. Living costs in Warsaw graphic There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe , while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year. Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU. For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France , but the gap is closing. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled. Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services. “The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.” Capitals salaries graphic He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious . Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support . Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement. “People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says. “In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.” As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs , an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day. There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany. On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077 , the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers. Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers. “In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.” Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.” Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back. “We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country. “We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more.
